extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or beginning graduate students studying real analysis / measure theory and ordinary differential equations
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and constructive methods for Lebesgue measure and measurable functions, together with surrounding results in ordinary differential equations (Frobenius/Bessel solutions and existence theorems). Suitable for learning/teaching and for writing rigorous solutions in these topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra / σ-algebra / Ring / σ-ring of sets (closure properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: An algebra of sets is a collection of subsets of X containing ∅ and X and closed under union and complement; a σ-algebra is an algebra closed under countable unions; a ring is closed under finite unions and set difference; a σ-ring is a ring closed under countable unions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these closure properties to decide which operations preserve measurability. The text notes symmetric difference and intersection are expressible from these operations and are used in proofs; one may form the smallest such class containing a given family by intersection of all containing classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure is a nonnegative completely additive (countably additive) set function defined on a σ-ring of subsets of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely: µ: R → [0, +∞] is completely additive if µ(∪_{n} E_n) = ∑_{n} µ(E_n) for pairwise disjoint E_n in R. When doing integration one normally works with a σ-algebra so constant functions are measurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity and basic properties of additive set functions (Proposition 5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ρ is additive on a ring R then it satisfies (a) finite additivity across N disjoint sets, (b) decomposition formula ρ(E ∪ F) = ρ(E) + ρ(F) − ρ(E ∩ F) (with caveats if values are infinite), (c) monotonicity when finite valued, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these algebraic identities to derive monotonicity, subadditivity, and continuity statements. The proposition lists consequences used repeatedly: ρ(E) ≤ ρ(E ∪ F) ≤ ρ(E) + ρ(F) and if ρ is nonnegative then E ⊆ F ⇒ ρ(E) ≤ ρ(F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of complete additivity via increasing sequences (Proposition 5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: An additive set function ρ on a ring R is completely additive iff for every increasing sequence E_n in R with union E (also in R) we have lim_{n→∞} ρ(E_n) = ρ(E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a practical continuity-from-below test: verify complete additivity by checking limit behavior on increasing sequences. The proof reduces a union of disjoint sets to an increasing sequence and uses additivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity from above on algebras (Corollary 5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: On an algebra A, if ρ is completely additive then for any decreasing sequence E_n in A with intersection E we have lim ρ(E_n) = ρ(E). Conversely, if lim ρ(E_n) = 0 whenever E_n is a decreasing sequence in A with empty intersection, then ρ is completely additive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the usual continuity-from-above statement for finite-measure situations; the corollary is used to check additivity by examining decreasing sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure space, σ-finiteness and finiteness (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure space is (X, A, µ) where A is a σ-algebra on X and µ a measure on A. It is σ-finite if X is a countable union of sets of finite µ-measure; finite if µ(X) < +∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: σ-finiteness is the central finiteness hypothesis for many extension and uniqueness theorems (e.g., the Extension Theorem). Many standard spaces (R with Lebesgue measure) are σ-finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension Theorem (existence and uniqueness of extension from a ring)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∫ is a nonnegative completely additive set function on a ring R that is σ-finite on R (i.e., X is contained in a countable union of members of R with finite ∫), then ∫ extends uniquely to a measure µ on the smallest σ-ring containing R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniqueness requires σ-finiteness (otherwise multiple extensions can exist). This theorem is applied to extend Lebesgue measure from elementary sets (finite unions of bounded intervals) to the Borel σ-algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and construction of Lebesgue measure on elementary sets
rubrics_metrics.description: On the ring of elementary sets (finite disjoint unions of bounded intervals) define m(E) as the sum of interval lengths. This definition is unambiguous and gives a nonnegative additive set function; one shows complete additivity on the ring (Proposition 5.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove unambiguity by reorganizing interval unions into disjoint ordered lists. To get a full measure on a σ-algebra, apply the Extension Theorem using σ-finiteness. Regularity (approximation by compact subsets from inside and open supersets from outside) is used in proofs of complete additivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity of Lebesgue measure on elementary sets (inner/outer approximation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given E an elementary set and ε>0, there exist compact K ⊆ E and open U ⊇ E with m(U) − m(K) arbitrarily small (inner regularity on elementary sets and approximation by open sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text constructs K and U for each bounded interval and then for unions of intervals, using compactness to pass from countable unions to finite subcovers. Regularity is used in proving complete additivity (Proposition 5.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard examples of measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include: (i) discrete weighted measures on a countable X (sum of weights over E); (ii) counting measure µ(E) = number of points in E (∈ N ∪ {+∞}); (iii) Lebesgue measure m defined on elementary sets and extended to Borel sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These models show the range of possible behaviors (finite, σ-finite, +∞ values) and are useful test-cases when checking hypotheses like σ-finiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurable function (equivalent inverse-image definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f: X → R* is measurable if f^{-1}((−∞, c)) (equivalently any of f^{-1}((−∞, c]), f^{-1}((c, +∞]), f^{-1}([c, +∞))) is measurable for every real c. These four formulations are equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving measurability, pick the inverse-image criterion convenient for the problem; use the algebraic manipulations of inverse images to move between interval types (countable unions/intersections arguments are used).

rubrics_metrics.name: Borel vs Lebesgue measurability and illustrative examples
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is the Borel σ-algebra on R, continuous functions are Borel measurable. Functions continuous except at countably many points are also Borel measurable. There exist Riemann integrable functions (extended by 0 off bounded interval) that are not Borel measurable, but they are Lebesgue measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuity and countability-of-exceptions to prove Borel measurability via inverse images of open sets. For Lebesgue measurability one uses the Lebesgue σ-algebra; the text indicates not every Riemann integrable function is Borel measurable (see Problem 33).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure properties of measurable functions (Proposition 5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant functions are measurable. If f is measurable then inverse images of intervals and open sets are measurable. The positive and negative parts f^+, f^− and the absolute value |f| are measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These closure properties are the building blocks for further algebraic operations on measurable functions (sums, products) and for constructing simple function approximations. The proposition gives the straightforward verifications using inverse-image criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frobenius method and Bessel equation solution criteria (series/Frobenius)
rubrics_metrics.description: For second-order linear ODEs with a regular singular point (example: Bessel's equation), substitute y = t^{s} ∑ c_n t^{n} to obtain the indicial equation and recurrence for c_n. For Bessel's equation the indicial equation gives s = ±p; if p is an integer complications arise (second solution may involve log t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the standard Frobenius algorithm: compute indicial equation from lowest-power terms, find possible s; derive recursion for coefficients c_n; inspect denominator zeros to detect resonance (roots differing by an integer) and deduce when a logarithmic second solution appears (the text references Problems 18–19 to identify the alternate form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Peano existence theorem constructive method
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove local existence for y' = F(t, y) with only continuity of F, construct polygonal approximations (Euler polygonals) using partitions with step ≤ min(δ, δ/M) where δ is the uniform continuity modulus on a rectangle R. Show the approximations are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous, apply Ascoli to extract a uniformly convergent subsequence, and show the limit is a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: choose δ for uniform continuity of F on the compact set R; define piecewise linear approximants y_n using the partition; prove equicontinuity and uniform boundedness (Problem 21–24); use Ascoli (Problem 25) to get a limit and verify it satisfies the integral equation y(t) = y0 + ∫_{t0}^{t} F(s, y(s)) ds. This shows existence without Lipschitz conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of variables / Fourier method for harmonic functions in unit disk (representation and Poisson kernel)
rubrics_metrics.description: A harmonic function u in the unit disk written in polar coordinates v(r,θ) can be expanded as ∑_{n=−∞}^{∞} c_n(r) e^{inθ}. For fixed r<1 and any δ>0 the Fourier series is absolutely convergent; Fourier coefficients have decay bounds (|c_n(r)| ≤ M/n^2 for 0 ≤ r ≤ 1−δ). Using convolution and the Poisson kernel one obtains the representation of harmonic functions via boundary data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 10–13 outline the separation-of-variables approach and how convolution with the Poisson kernel recovers harmonic functions from boundary values; use boundedness estimates and absolute convergence to justify manipulations and to relate to the Poisson integral formula.
